title: The sharp shape-parameter law for sinh and Kaiser–Bessel regularised Shannon sampling, with a corrected alias-inclusive error bound
shortTitle: Tuning the window: the sharp law
oneLine: For windowed sinc reconstruction with the sinh and Kaiser–Bessel windows, the error decays fastest exactly when the shape parameter grows like dm, as Kircheis, Potts and Tasche conjectured; over-tuning costs far more than under-tuning, a gap in the general error estimate is corrected, and the published explicit bounds survive.
abstract: Regularised (windowed) Shannon sampling rebuilds a bandlimited signal from its 2m nearest integer samples by multiplying the cardinal sine by a compactly supported window. The sinh-type and continuous Kaiser–Bessel (cKB) windows, which are also standard kernels of nonuniform fast Fourier transforms and gridding, each have a shape parameter β. For signals of angular bandwidth δ < π put d = π − δ. Kircheis, Potts and Tasche (BIT Numer. Math. 2025) conjectured that β = dm gives the maximal exponential decay of the error. This candidate proves that the worst-case error over the L² unit ball satisfies log E = −β + √((β² − d²m²)₊) + O(log m) uniformly in β > 0, for both windows, so the optimal exponential rate is d and is attained, in that rate sense, exactly when β/m → d. Under-tuning loses accuracy linearly and over-tuning like a square root. The same law holds for each signal whose spectrum has bounded variation and is bounded away from zero, while exact optimality of dm at finite m fails. Leading constants, a second-order sinh tuning law and family minima are given. The general error estimate used for these windows since 2022 omits aliased bands: an exact rational certificate violates it by a factor of about 3500. An alias-inclusive replacement is proved for a narrower window class containing both windows, and the published explicit sinh and cKB bounds are shown to remain true. Optimal pointwise linear recovery from the same samples has root-limsup rate tan²(δ/4), a larger exponent than either window attains. Certified interval-arithmetic tables give the finite-m picture for m ≤ 32. A two-term law for the slow cKB convergence is stated as a conjecture. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Worst-case law, both windows: log E = −β + √((β² − d²m²)₊) + O(log m) uniformly in β > 0, so the optimal exponential rate is d and is attained exactly when β/m → d; under-tuning loses linearly, over-tuning like a square root (proof).

Per-signal law for spectra of bounded variation bounded away from zero, covering the source's test signal; exact finite-m optimality of β = dm fails for both windows (proof; certified finite-m tables).

The general error estimate used since 2022 omits aliased bands: a certified exact-rational counterexample violates it by a factor of about 3500; an alias-inclusive replacement holds for a narrower window class, and the published explicit sinh and cKB bounds remain true (proof).
Optimal pointwise linear recovery from the same 2m samples has root-limsup rate tan²(δ/4), exponent 2 log cot(δ/4) > d (proof).
At twofold oversampling and 8 ≤ m ≤ 32, raising β by one above dm multiplies the error by 10–670 (sinh) or 3–220 (cKB); lowering it by one costs 2.1–3.1 (certified).

narration: The sharp shape-parameter law for windowed Shannon sampling. An Evidence Press briefing. Many instruments record a continuous signal only at regularly spaced moments, and software must rebuild the signal in between. The classical recipe adds up shifted wave-shaped copies, but in practice only nearby samples are used, each softened by a window. The same windows are used inside the fast Fourier methods behind MRI scanners and radio telescopes. Two popular windows each have one tuning knob, called the shape parameter. In 2025, Kircheis, Potts and Tasche conjectured that one simple setting of this knob gives the fastest possible gain in accuracy as more samples are used. This release proves their conjecture for the worst-case error, and finds the exact law behind it. Setting the knob too low loses accuracy gently, in proportion to the shortfall. Setting it too high loses accuracy much faster, like a square root. With twofold oversampling, one unit too high can multiply the error by as much as several hundred, while one unit too low costs a factor of only two or three. So if in doubt, err low. The release also finds a gap in a general error estimate used in this line of work since 2022: it leaves out aliased frequencies. A corrected bound is proved, and the published explicit error bounds for the two windows turn out to be true. Finally, the best possible linear method using the same samples does better than either window. The proofs are written out, and the numerical tables are certified with rigorous arithmetic. This is an anonymous, unrefereed candidate, checked only by AI-assisted review, and not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on 21 October 2026, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: A two-sided worst-case error law for sinh and continuous Kaiser–Bessel windowed Shannon sampling, uniform in the shape parameter, settling the worst-case reading of the Kircheis–Potts–Tasche optimality conjectures; with a certified counterexample to their general estimate, an alias-inclusive replacement and confirmation of the published explicit bounds.
decisionObject.scope: Exact, noiseless integer samples; fixed bandwidth δ < π; worst case over the L² unit ball of the Paley–Wiener space and the evaluation point; per-signal law for spectra of bounded variation bounded away from zero; certified tables only in their finite ranges. No noise, finite-precision, varying-bandwidth or deconvolved-NFFT result.
